description: We are CS graduates who build AI and data systems and want to aim those skills at space for a weekend. We have shipped ML models and web apps, and we finish what we start. We lean toward data-heavy challenges. Looking for a science mind, a designer, and a presenter who can sell the project in three minutes.
summary:
A lunar base is expected to keep its air at 30% oxygen or more. NASA has burned solid materials in orbit many times, but never above 22.2% oxygen. We built Flame in Freefall to make that gap easy to see and to show what the existing data can still tell a habitat designer.
The site reads all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and turns their 21 test tables into one table of 2,127 rows. Every oxygen and pressure value is marked as measured, planned or assumed. Pick a habitat, such as the ISS, a lunar base, a pressurized rover or a Mars habitat, and the investigations are ranked by how close their tests came to that cabin. A cabin lab plots every test against an oxygen and pressure you choose. You can also ask questions in plain English, and each answer about the data cites the NASA record it came from.
Only 20 tests in the whole record ran at lunar-base conditions, and all of them were gas flames. Before crews live on the Moon, someone has to burn solids in that air. The site ends by naming four experiments that would close the gap.
details:
What it does

NASA has flown dozens of fire experiments in orbit, and their results sit in PSI as 24 investigations, 21 experimental tables and more than 82,000 raw files. That is a lot to dig through if all you want to know is how a fabric burns at 30% oxygen. Flame in Freefall puts the answer in one place.

The home page walks through the problem in one scroll. NASA's candle flame loses gravity and turns from a teardrop into a blue dome, and then the gap appears in two numbers: 22.2% for the highest solid test and 30% for a lunar cabin. The Evidence page holds the detail. It has an oxygen ruler for each fuel type, a map of every test by oxygen and pressure, the SAFFIRE-II results for the same materials burned in microgravity and on Earth, three reviewed briefs, and four experiments we think should fly next.

In the cabin lab you set oxygen, pressure, fuel and gravity for a cabin, or start from a habitat or from one of the two cabin atmospheres NASA's BRE record lists for human missions. The map then shows which tests fall near your cabin and how they ended. Nothing there is a prediction, and the flame is drawn solid only where tests exist.

Rank scores the 24 investigations for a chosen habitat. Three sliders weight prevention, detection and suppression, and each row explains its score in two sentences. Investigations and Compare let you read each study and set up to four side by side. Ask, and Wisp, a small guide that sits on every page, take questions in plain English, and answers about the data cite the NASA record behind them. Back on Earth lists the uses the investigations name for themselves, such as smoke detectors for submarines and cleaner engines.

What the data shows

No solid-material test in PSI ran above 22.2% oxygen. Those 140 tests come from BASS-II, SAFFIRE-I and SAFFIRE-II.

Only 20 tests ran at lunar-base conditions (30% oxygen or more at 70 kPa or less). All 20 were gas flames in ACME CFI-G.

Gravity can reverse the result. In SAFFIRE-II, thin silicone burned completely on Earth and barely at all in microgravity, while a cotton-fiberglass fabric burned its full 29 cm in both.

How it works

A Python pipeline pulls the investigations from NASA's public PSI API. It downloads under 1 MB and leaves the 16 TB of video and sensor files on NASA's servers, linked from each page. It converts 21 tables recorded in mmHg, atm, bar, percent and mole fraction into one table of 2,127 rows. Each oxygen and pressure value carries a tag for measured, planned or assumed, so an assumed cabin value never shows up as a test condition.

The ranking is plain arithmetic with no model involved. It weighs how close the tests came to the habitat (35%), whether the study covers the pillar you care about (25%), how relevant the material is (20%) and how much data exists (20%). The same formula runs in Python and in the browser, and a test checks that all 120 scores agree.

Open-weight models (GPT-OSS on Groq) write the plain summaries, the ranking reasons and the answers. They only see facts the code has already computed or passages retrieved from NASA's text. Code then checks every number, rank, citation and oxygen claim against the tables. A reply that fails goes back once with its problems listed, and if it fails again the site shows a labelled fact-only version.

Benefits and impact

A habitat designer can see in a minute which experiments came closest to their cabin and how far the evidence falls short. Fire modelers get one clean table in common units, downloadable as CSV. For planners, the site lists what is missing and four concrete experiments to close it. Every number links back to its NASA record, so anyone can check a claim. When partial-gravity results from LUCI and FM2 reach PSI, the same pipeline can place them on the map.

What we considered

We kept measured and assumed values apart everywhere, because mixing them would overstate what NASA has tested. The models only see facts the code gives them, and code rejects their mistakes. In review this caught real errors, including a draft that claimed no solid had been tested in microgravity. We also found and fixed an error of our own: inverse-flame tests had been counted at the oxygen of the burner stream, which raised the lunar count from 20 to 66. PSI has no partial-gravity combustion data yet, and the Mars habitat atmosphere is our assumption, labelled as such on the site.

Tools

Python, pandas, FastAPI and rank-bm25 for the pipeline and the API, which runs on Render. Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Motion and hand-built SVG charts for the site, which runs on GitHub Pages. GPT-OSS 20B and 120B through Groq. Every change runs through GitHub Actions with Python unittest, Vitest, ESLint and TypeScript.
